name: Marathi
where: Maharashtra (Mumbai, Pune, Nagpur), Goa, and Marathi communities across India and abroad
tagline: The language of Mumbai, Pune and Maharashtra — a thousand-year literary tradition, and the key to everyday life in India's richest state.
intro:
**Marathi** (मराठी) is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by around 90 million people, mostly in the western Indian state of Maharashtra. It is the official language of the state, the everyday language of Pune, the home language of a huge share of Mumbai, and has a written tradition stretching back to the 13th-century saint-poet Dnyaneshwar.

Marathi is written in **Devanagari**, the same script as Hindi and Nepali, with a few extras: the retroflex lateral **ळ**, the 'eyelash' र (ऱ्य), and the letters **ॲ / ऑ** for English sounds. Many words look familiar to anyone who knows Hindi, but the grammar is distinctly its own: three genders (masculine, feminine, **neuter**), case endings that glue onto the noun (घर*ात* 'in the house', मुंबई*ला* 'to Mumbai'), and verbs that change for the gender of the speaker — a man says मी जातो, a woman says मी जाते ('I go').

Register matters. **तू** is intimate/informal 'you', **तुम्ही** is the normal polite 'you' (and plural), and **आपण** is very formal 'you' — though in everyday speech आपण more often means inclusive 'we' (you and I). This course teaches the standard spoken Marathi of Pune and Mumbai, pointing out the colloquial forms you will actually hear (e.g. written करणे vs spoken करणं, written आहे vs spoken 'ए/य' contractions).

You'll start with greetings and build up through 20 units to telling stories, handling problems and holding real conversations.
romanizationNote: The romanization shows how Marathi is **pronounced**, not just spelled. Long vowels have a macron (ā ī ū); plain e and o are always long-ish, as in 'café' and 'go'. Dots under letters mark retroflex sounds (ṭ ḍ ṇ ḷ) made with the tongue curled back; plain t d n are dental (tongue on the teeth). An h after a consonant means a puff of breath (kh, ph, th, bh), never English 'th' or 'f'. **Important Marathi point:** च ज झ have two pronunciations, and the romanization shows which one: **ts dz dzh** for the dental sounds (चार tsār 'four', माझा mādzhā 'my') and **ch j jh** for the palatal ones as in English 'church', 'jam' (चिमणी chimṇī 'sparrow', जेवण jevaṇ 'meal'). æ is the 'a' of 'cat' (ॲ, बॅग bæg), ô is the 'o' of British 'hot' (ऑ, ऑफिस ôfis). ṃ marks a nasalized vowel, e.g. the colloquial neuter ending in केलं kelaṃ ('did'), which sounds like a short nasal 'uh'.

script.overview:
Marathi uses **Devanagari** (देवनागरी), here in its Marathi form called **Balbodh** (बाळबोध). It is an **abugida**: every consonant letter carries a built-in short vowel 'a' (क = ka). To write another vowel after a consonant you add a **vowel sign** (matra): क + ा = का kā, क + ि = कि ki, क + े = के ke. Vowels have separate full forms (अ आ इ ई…) used at the start of a word or after another vowel.

Writing runs left to right and letters hang from a horizontal **headline** (शिरोरेखा) that joins the letters of a word. Write the letter body first, then draw the headline across the whole word.

To write a consonant with **no** vowel, add the **virama** (्): क् = k. When two consonants meet with no vowel between them they usually fuse into a **conjunct** (जोडाक्षर): क् + ष = क्ष, त् + र = त्र, स् + त = स्त. A few conjuncts look nothing like their parts (क्ष, ज्ञ), so learn them as units.

Marathi has some features that differ from Hindi: the extra letter **ळ** (ḷ); the **eyelash र** (ऱ्य, as in चौऱ्याहत्तर 'seventy-four' and ऱ्हस्व), written instead of the normal half-र before य and ह in certain words; **ॲ** and **ऑ** (and the signs ॅ ॉ) for English loanwords like बॅग 'bag' and ऑफिस 'office'; and the convention that a final i or u in native words is written long (ी ू). The inherent 'a' is often not pronounced at the end of a word or in the middle of native words (see the pronunciation section on schwa deletion), and **च ज झ** each have two pronunciations that the script does not distinguish.

Marathi also uses its own **Devanagari digits** (० १ २ ३ ४ ५ ६ ७ ८ ९), which you will see on signs, calendars and in newspapers, alongside Western digits.

groups.note: Used on signs, calendars, bus numbers and newspapers. Place value works exactly as with Western digits: २०२६ = 2026.

pronunciation.title: The two sounds of च ज झ
pronunciation.body:
This is the most distinctive feature of Marathi pronunciation. Each of the letters **च ज झ** stands for two different sounds:

**Dental (ts, dz, dzh):** the tongue tip touches the back of the upper teeth, giving 'ts' as in 'cats', 'dz' as in 'adze'. This is the default in native Marathi words, especially before a, ā, u, ū, o: चार tsār 'four', चहा tsahā 'tea', जागा dzāgā 'place', माझा mādzhā 'my', आज ādz 'today'. झ often sounds almost like a 'z'.

**Palatal (ch, j, jh):** as in English 'church', 'jam'. Used (1) before i, ī, e, ai and y: चिमणी chimṇī 'sparrow', जेवण jevaṇ 'meal', खुर्ची khurchī 'chair'; and (2) in most words borrowed from Sanskrit, Hindi and English, whatever the vowel: जय jay 'victory', चर्चा charchā 'discussion', जानेवारी jānevārī 'January', चॉकलेट chôkleṭ.

The script doesn't show the difference, so this course's romanization does. Using 'ch/j' everywhere won't stop people understanding you, but it is the clearest mark of a non-native (or Hindi) accent. **छ** is always palatal (chh).
tips: Say 'cats' and freeze on the 'ts' — that is Marathi च in चार.
The vowel decides: चोर tsor 'thief' but चित्र chitra 'picture'; जात dzāt 'going' but जीव jīv 'life'.
If a word looks Sanskrit, English or Hindi (जनता, चर्चा, जून), use the palatal sound.
माझा, तुझा, झाले: let झ be a buzzy 'dz-h', close to 'z'.

pairs.note: ts before a; ch before i.
dz before ā; j before e.
Same vowel, but जय is a Sanskrit word and keeps the palatal j.
dzh before ā; jh before e.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex vs dental consonants
pronunciation.body:
Marathi distinguishes two sets of t/d/n sounds that English lumps together.

**Dental** त थ द ध न: put the tip of the tongue against the back of your upper front teeth. The result is softer and 'flatter' than English t, like French or Spanish t.

**Retroflex** ट ठ ड ढ ण: curl the tip of the tongue back and strike the roof of the mouth behind the gum ridge. The result is hollow and 'thick'.

English t and d fall between the two, so Marathi speakers hear English t as retroflex (they write 'table' as टेबल). Your job is to push dental sounds forward to the teeth and retroflex sounds clearly back. Mixing them up changes words: सात sāt 'seven' vs साठ sāṭh 'sixty'.
tips: For त/द, let your tongue tip actually touch your teeth — you should feel it.
For ट/ड, curl the tongue back until the underside nearly touches the palate.
Practise in pairs: say सात then साठ, आत then आठ.
ण is the retroflex n — the same curled tongue, with air through the nose.

pairs.note: Not a minimal pair: compare the d sounds at the start.

pronunciation.title: Aspiration: k vs kh, b vs bh
pronunciation.body:
Every stop comes in pairs: plain and **aspirated** (with a puff of breath). In English, the 'p' in 'pin' is aspirated and the 'p' in 'spin' isn't, but English speakers never have to control it. In Marathi it changes meaning: गाव gāv 'village', घाव ghāv 'wound'.

The plain sounds (क त प ट च) have **no** puff — hold your hand in front of your mouth and you should feel almost nothing. The aspirated voiceless sounds (ख थ फ ठ छ) have a strong puff. The voiced aspirates (घ ध भ ढ झ) are 'breathy': say the consonant with a murmur of h, as in 'doghouse', 'clubhouse'.

Remember: थ and ध are never English 'th'; फ is often pronounced 'f' in modern speech, which is fine.
tips: Hold a tissue in front of your lips: it should stay still for प and flutter for फ.
For भ, घ, ध say 'abhor', 'doghouse', 'adhere' and keep the breath with the consonant.
Don't aspirate English-style: Marathi क in कप is like the k in 'skip'.

pronunciation.title: ळ — the Marathi retroflex L
pronunciation.body:
**ळ** (ḷ) is one of the most frequent sounds in Marathi and it does not exist in standard Hindi. Make it by curling the tongue tip back as for ड and then letting air flow round the sides as for l. It sounds like a 'dark', hollow l.

It contrasts with ordinary dental-alveolar **ल**: काळ kāḷ 'time, era' vs काल kāl 'yesterday', वेळ veḷ 'time, occasion' vs वेल vel 'creeper (plant)'. Very common words have it: शाळा 'school', डोळा 'eye', सकाळ 'morning', पोळी 'flatbread', केळ 'banana', मुळे 'because of', सगळा 'all'.
tips: Say ड, keep the tongue curled, and change it to an 'l' — that's ळ.
Don't replace ळ with 'r' or plain 'l'; Marathi speakers notice immediately.
In romanized Marathi online you'll see ळ written as 'l' or 'L' (e.g. 'shaLa').

pronunciation.title: ण vs न
pronunciation.body:
**ण** is the retroflex n: curl the tongue back exactly as for ट and let the air out through the nose. **न** is dental, with the tongue on the teeth.

ण is everywhere in Marathi — far more than in Hindi. Every infinitive ends in -णे (करणे 'to do', जाणे 'to go'), the future-intent forms use -णार (येणार 'will come'), and everyday words like पाणी 'water', कोण 'who', पण 'but', आणि 'and' all have it. ण never begins a word.
tips: Practise ट-ण-ट-ण with the tongue staying curled.
Endings: करणे, जाणार, खाणं — all retroflex.
In Hindi पानी has न; Marathi पाणी has ण.

pronunciation.title: The silent 'a': schwa deletion in Marathi
pronunciation.body:
Every consonant letter carries a short 'a', but it isn't always pronounced.

**1. Word-final:** the final 'a' is silent: घर ghar (not ghara), कमळ kamaḷ, आज ādz. **Exception:** it is kept after a conjunct: मित्र mitra, धर्म dharma, प्रश्न prashna.

**2. Inside native words and verb forms:** in a sequence a-C-a-C-vowel, the second 'a' usually drops: बसला → baslā, करतो → karto, सगळा → sagḷā, कपडे → kapḍe, समजला → samadzlā.

**3. How Marathi differs from Hindi:** in **Sanskrit (tatsama) words**, Marathi keeps the medial 'a' where Hindi drops it. Hindi says kalpnā, bhāvnā, ghaṭnā, rachnā, janatā→jantā; Marathi says **kalpanā, bhāvanā, ghaṭanā, rachanā, janatā**. So the same spelling can be pronounced differently in the two languages, and saying 'kalpnā' in Marathi sounds Hindi-influenced.

**4. Colloquial endings:** the written neuter ending -े in verbs and adjectives is pronounced -ं in speech: आले → आलं ālaṃ 'it came', करणे → करणं karṇaṃ. Modern informal writing increasingly spells it this way.
tips: Don't add an 'a' at the end of a word unless it ends in a conjunct.
In verb forms (बसलो, करतात, चालला) squeeze the middle a out.
In 'learned' Sanskrit words (घटना, कल्पना, सूचना, जनता) pronounce every a.

pairs.note: The a after स disappears when a suffix is added.
Final a silent vs kept after a conjunct.
Native verb: a dropped. Sanskrit word: a kept (Hindi: kalpnā).

pronunciation.title: Anusvara and nasal vowels
pronunciation.body:
The dot above (ं, anusvara) has several pronunciations depending on what follows.

**Before a stop consonant** it becomes the nasal of the same mouth position: आंबा āmbā 'mango' (m before b), घंटा ghaṇṭā 'bell' (ṇ before ṭ), पंख paṅkh 'wing' (ṅ before kh), हिंदी hindī.

**Before य र ल व श ष स ह** and at the end of a word it **nasalizes the vowel**: हंस haṃs 'swan', सिंह siṃha 'lion'.

**In colloquial endings** (spoken -ं for written -े): कसं kasaṃ 'how', केलं kelaṃ 'did', बरं baraṃ 'OK': here it is a short, lightly nasal 'uh', and it marks the **neuter** gender. So कसा (m), कशी (f), कसं (n) are three different forms.
tips: Don't pronounce the dot as a separate 'm' unless a b/p/m follows.
The neuter -ं is short and soft — kelaṃ, not 'kelam'.
Listen for the gender: आला (he came), आली (she came), आलं (it came).

pronunciation.title: Vowel length
pronunciation.body:
Marathi has short and long vowel pairs: अ/आ, इ/ई, उ/ऊ. The **a/ā** contrast is the important one: अ is a short neutral 'uh' (as in 'about'), आ is a long open 'ah' (as in 'father'). These are different vowels, not just different lengths, and confusing them changes words: दर dar 'rate', दार dār 'door'.

For **i/ī** and **u/ū**, the difference is real in careful speech but small in everyday conversation. Spelling rules also play a role: in native Marathi words a final i or u is always written long (पाणी, लाडू), even though it sounds medium.

ए and ओ are always long-ish and pure (no glide).
tips: अ is NOT the 'a' in 'cat' — it is the relaxed 'uh' in 'but'.
Give आ its full length: kār, dār, kāp.
Don't diphthongise ए/ओ: 'pet-e', not 'pay-ee'.

pronunciation.title: ज्ञ, क्ष, ऋ and श/ष
pronunciation.body:
A few letters are pronounced in a specifically Marathi way.

**ज्ञ** is pronounced **'dny'** in Marathi (Hindi says 'gy'): ज्ञान dnyān 'knowledge', विज्ञान vidnyān 'science', the saint ज्ञानेश्वर Dnyāneshvar. You will see this in English spellings like 'Dnyaneshwar'.

**ऋ / ृ** is pronounced **'ru'** (Hindi 'ri'): कृपया krupayā 'please', गृहपाठ gruhapāṭh 'homework', ऋतू rutū 'season'.

**श** and **ष** are both 'sh' in everyday Marathi: शाळा shāḷā, भाषा bhāṣā (said 'bhāshā'). **क्ष** = 'ksh'.
tips: Practise 'dny' as one quick onset: dnyān.
कृ = kru, not kri: कृपया krupayā.
Don't worry about श vs ष — say both as 'sh'.

pairs.note: श and ष sound the same in Marathi.

pronunciation.title: English sounds: ॲ and ऑ
pronunciation.body:
Marathi borrows English words freely (बस, ट्रेन, ऑफिस, मोबाईल) and has two special vowels for them.

**ॲ / ॅ** (æ) is the 'a' in 'cat', 'bank': बॅग bæg, बँक bæṅk, कॅप kæp. Without the moon, plain अ would be 'uh': कप kap 'cup'.

**ऑ / ॉ** (ô) is the 'o' in British 'hot', 'office': ऑफिस ôfis, डॉक्टर ḍôkṭar, कॉलेज kôlej. Plain ओ is the long 'o' in 'go'.

English t and d become retroflex ट ड (टेबल, डॉक्टर) and English 'th' becomes थ or द.
tips: The little moon (ॅ ॉ) above a letter = English vowel.
Pronounce English loans the Marathi way: ṭ and ḍ for t and d.
Many speakers say 'f' for फ in loans: फोन fon.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants
pronunciation.body:
A doubled consonant (written as a conjunct of the same letter: त्त, क्क, ल्ल, प्प) is **held longer**, with a tiny pause before release, like the 'tt' across 'hot tea' or 'kk' in 'book-case'. Doubling is meaningful and very common in numbers and everyday words: सत्तर sattar 'seventy', पत्ता pattā 'address', गप्पा gappā 'chat', अक्का akkā 'elder sister'.

English speakers tend to shorten these. Hold the closure for about twice as long as a single consonant.
tips: Think 'hot-tea' for त्त in पत्ता: pat-tā.
Don't add a vowel between the doubled consonants.
Numbers are a great drill: बत्तीस, छत्तीस, पन्नास, सत्तर, नव्वद.

pronunciation.title: Rhythm, stress and question intonation
pronunciation.body:
Marathi has no strong word stress like English; syllables are given fairly even weight, with long vowels (ā ī ū e o) and syllables before double consonants sounding a little heavier. Don't reduce unstressed vowels to 'uh' the way English does.

**Yes/no questions** are made in two ways: with rising intonation on the last word (तू येणार? 'You're coming?'), or by adding the particle **का** at the end with a rise: तू येणार आहेस का? 'Are you coming?' **Question-word questions** (काय, कोण, कुठे) usually fall at the end.

Sentence-final particles colour meaning: **ना** (softening / 'right?'), **ग / रे** (addressing a woman / man familiarly), **हं** (agreement).
tips: Keep vowels full: 'mu-la-gā', not 'm'lga'.
For a yes/no question add का and let your voice rise.
रे to a male friend, ग to a female friend: काय रे? / काय ग?
